title: One dose of acid, two liquids
hook: The same acid goes into two clear liquids. Why does only one barely notice?

knows: that pH is a log scale: one unit is a factor of 10 in hydrogen ions (the pH lesson)
that lower pH is more acidic
doesNotKnow: why some solutions barely change pH when acid is added

misconception: The same amount of acid always changes the pH by the same amount, whatever it is added to.
objective: The learner can explain that a buffer holds a stock of base that turns added hydrogen ions into weak acid, so the acid/base ratio and the pH barely move: 0.010 mol of strong acid drops 1 L of water from pH 7 to 2 but the acetate buffer only from 4.76 to 4.67.

claims.text: Acetic acid has a pKa of about 4.76 at 25 °C, so a buffer with equal amounts of acetic acid and acetate starts at pH 4.76.
claims.source: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 'Dissociation constants of organic acids and bases': acetic acid pKa 4.756 at 25 °C. Equal amounts give log10(1) = 0, so pH = pKa.

claims.text: A buffer's pH follows the ratio of base to acid: pH = pKa + log10([acetate]/[acetic acid]).
claims.source: Henderson-Hasselbalch equation; Atkins & de Paula, Physical Chemistry (acid-base equilibria), or Harris, Quantitative Chemical Analysis, ch. 8. Valid here because both concentrations stay far above [H+].

claims.text: After 0.010 mol of strong acid the buffer ratio is 0.09 : 0.11 and its pH is about 4.67, a fall of under 0.1.
claims.source: Each H+ converts one acetate to acetic acid: acetate 0.10 - 0.010 = 0.090, acid 0.10 + 0.010 = 0.110 mol/L. pH = 4.76 + log10(0.090/0.110) = 4.76 - 0.087 = 4.673 (node script).

claims.text: 0.010 mol of strong acid in 1 L of pure water takes it from pH 7 to pH 2, five units; the first 0.001 mol alone takes it to pH 3.
claims.source: Strong acid dissociates fully: [H+] = 0.010 mol/L, pH = 2.00; at 0.001 mol, pH = 3.00. Stage solves [H+] = n + Kw/[H+] with Kw = 1.0e-14 at 25 °C (pure water starts at pH 7.00). Ignores dissolved CO2, which makes real 'pure' water slightly acidic.

claims.text: The lesson ignores the small volume the acid itself adds (each 0.001 mol dose is treated as adding no volume to the litre).
claims.source: Modelling simplification stated on file. With concentrated acid (e.g. 12 mol/L HCl, 0.083 mL per dose) the volume error is under 0.1%.

claims.text: Blood is buffered and stays near pH 7.4.
claims.source: Normal arterial blood pH 7.35-7.45, held mainly by the bicarbonate buffer: Hall, Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed., ch. 31 (acid-base regulation).

recall.question: Why does a buffer's pH barely move when a little strong acid is added?
options: Its stock of base soaks up the acid
recall.why: The buffer's base turns each added hydrogen ion into weak acid; pH follows the base-to-acid ratio, which shifts only slightly.
